rationale: CheckRun dd6a5001bf7f487994e7ec6dd674bb02 returned completed/tests_passed with exit 0 and 21 parsed CA_EVENT observations with 0 parsing errors. Indices 17-19 are the three rejection operands the last revision added and index 20 is the summary; I interpret them for @joint_apply_order, and they force a split verdict: the entry is identical each time (index 4, term 2, one change, joint-entering) but the surrounding state is not what the lag hypothesis predicted, because every rejecting node reports applied=4 and committed=4 at the moment the Changer rejects, i.e. the node was not behind on application. That leaves two readings alive - a target-side shape in which a joint-entering change reaches a node whose tracker is joint with no application lag involved, or a harness artifact in which the same entry is applied with an applied index that already covers its own index (which would be a double application or an off-by-one in the harness's apply bookkeeping, and looks exactly like applied == entry index) - and I will not choose between them without the extra operands. The interpretation therefore stays unresolved, records the narrowed explanation, and names the discriminator that separates the two.

interpretations.rationale: The operands are consistent across all three occurrences: nodes 3, 1 and 4 (seed 35, steps 22, 23 and 31) each reject an entry at index 4, term 2, one change, requested joint transition, with joint_now=true and the reason 'config is already joint', and index 20 reports three such rejections in 245 configuration changes with violations=0. Two facts constrain the explanation and one observation blocks a verdict. First, the entry is the same in every occurrence, so the phenomenon is about one log position rather than about three independent proposals. Second, the rejecting nodes are not application-lagging at that moment: applied=4 and committed=4 in all three events, which refutes the lag-based reading the earlier interpretations relied on and also refutes my own earlier framing that the shape only arises when a node's application is behind. Third, and this is why I do not assert anything yet, applied equals the index of the entry being applied (4): that is precisely what a double application or an off-by-one in the harness's apply bookkeeping would produce, and the harness does rebuild nodes from persisted storage at restart events with Config.Applied taken from the node's applied index, so the possibility that the harness hands a node an entry it has already applied cannot be excluded from these four indices. The honest narrowing is therefore: either the target can present a joint-entering change to a node whose tracker is joint with no lag involved - which would be an availability-relevant shape caused by the log order rather than by application slowness - or the harness applies an entry whose index is already covered by its applied index, in which case the rejections are a harness artifact and the earlier refutation of the panic path stands. The discriminator is small and decisive: print, immediately before each apply batch, the node's applied and applying pointers and the batch's first and last entry indexes, and flag any batch whose first index is <= applied; if a batch re-applies an already-applied entry, the artifact is confirmed and the rejection count must be discarded, and if instead the batch starts at applied+1 for the rejecting node, the log genuinely carried a joint-entering change at that position while the node's tracker was joint.

knowledge.assertion: a node can be handed a joint-entering change while its own configuration is joint, with the propose-time guard bounding only what the leader appends given its own applied configuration

counterevidence: Index 20 shows violations=0 alongside the rejections, so whatever the cause, the four safety invariants held in the run that produced them.
All three rejections come from a single seed (seed 35) and a single entry (index 4, term 2), so they may reflect one configuration history rather than a general pattern.

The harness rebuilds nodes at restart events with Config.Applied set from the node's applied index, which is exactly the code path that could re-present entries to the application; that path was not instrumented for this receipt.
limitations: The receipt carries index, term, change count, joint flag, applied, committed and joint_now, but not the node's applying pointer, the batch boundaries, or the surrounding entries, so it cannot separate double application from a genuine log-order shape.
Targets exclude the current leader, so no rejection was observed at a leader, and the run covered one configuration shape at a time.
Only the first three occurrences emit operands while the counter counts all rejections, so a fourth occurrence with different operands would be invisible in this receipt.
